records.title: Scale-up capital: the EU's new equity instruments are starting to show up in the round data
records.summary: Between August and November 2026 the Scaleup Europe Fund became operational, ETCI 2.0 reached a first closing and an institutional investors pact was launched. In the funding data, an EU-level investor is named in 20 of the 222 disclosed rounds of €50M or more in the last 12 months, six of them involving the Scaleup Europe Fund.

sections.title: Background and objectives
sections.text: The 2025 Startup and Scaleup Strategy set out to close Europe's scale-up financing gap with a Scaleup Europe Fund and a pact with institutional investors. In 2026 both moved from announcement to operation, alongside a second edition of the EIB Group's European Tech Champions Initiative (ETCI).

sources.title: Scaleup Europe Fund
EIB Group: Commission and EIB launch Institutional Investors Pact

sections.title: Financial mechanisms
sections.text: Three routes coexist: direct equity from the EIC Fund (including STEP Scale Up tickets of €10–30M in rounds of €50–150M), the Scaleup Europe Fund (inside the EIC Fund, managed by EQT) investing directly in large rounds, and fund-of-funds commitments (ETCI) into large VC funds, which then invest in companies.

sources.title: EIC STEP Scale Up
Commission press release IP/26/1718: Scaleup Europe Fund operational
EIB Group: institutional investors and Member States to channel over €10bn into scale-ups

facts.text: The Scaleup Europe Fund was established as part of the EIC Fund with EQT as independent investment manager and a €5bn target; fundraising continues.

sources.title: Commission press release IP/26/1718: Scaleup Europe Fund operational

facts.text: Its first investment was co-leading ICEYE's €1bn financing round (announced 5 August 2026, subject to closing conditions).

sources.title: EQT: Scaleup Europe Fund co-leads ICEYE round (company press release)

facts.text: On 9 November 2026 the Tech Champions fund-of-funds (ETCI 2.0) reached a first closing of about €2bn with seven Member States, and 15 institutional investors declared an intention to channel more than €8bn. ETCI 1 has committed about €3.5bn to 15 large VC funds.

sources.title: EIB Group: institutional investors and Member States to channel over €10bn into scale-ups

facts.text: The European Institutional Investors Pact was launched on 22 September 2026 by the Commission and the EIB Group, with 13 institutional investors stating an intention to invest.

sources.title: EIB Group: Commission and EIB launch Institutional Investors Pact

facts.text: EIC STEP Scale Up invests €10–30M of equity in rounds of €50–150M; the next batch cut-off is 25 November 2026.

sources.title: EIC STEP Scale Up

calculations.text: In the 12 months to 9 November 2026 there were 222 disclosed venture rounds of €50M or more in Europe, totalling €50.1bn, or 71.5% of all disclosed venture euros.
calculations.method: Equity rounds (all stages except debt, grants, crowdfunding) with disclosed amount ≥ €50M, dated 10 Nov 2025 – 9 Nov 2026, in the 31 covered countries. Source: TechCap funding dataset (Tech.eu Funding Explorer, CC BY 4.0, plus multi-source confirmed rounds), disclosed rounds to 9 Nov 2026

calculations.text: 20 of those 222 rounds name an EU-level investor (EIC/EIC Fund, EIB, EIF, Scaleup Europe Fund or another EU programme). The Scaleup Europe Fund is named in six: Iceye, Lovable, The Exploration Company, Tandem Health, EUCLYD and Pigment.
calculations.method: Investor names matched against the EU-institution rules published in site/assets/policy-analytics.js. Source: TechCap funding dataset (Tech.eu Funding Explorer, CC BY 4.0, plus multi-source confirmed rounds), disclosed rounds to 9 Nov 2026

calculations.text: Within the STEP Scale Up ticket range (rounds of €50–150M), 9 of 144 rounds name an EU-level investor.
calculations.method: Same as above, restricted to disclosed amounts between €50M and €150M.

interpretation: EU instruments are now visible as named co-investors in large rounds, but they remain a minority presence: roughly one large round in eleven.
Most ETCI money will not appear in round data at all: it reaches companies through the VC funds it backs, so round-level counts understate the EU's role in late-stage financing.
hypotheses: If the Scaleup Europe Fund and STEP Scale Up deploy as planned, the share of ≥€50M rounds naming an EU investor should rise from about 9% over the next four quarters. This page will track it.

audiences.founders: Companies raising €50–150M can apply to STEP Scale Up (next cut-off 25 Nov 2026) and should expect EU-backed investors to co-invest alongside, not replace, private leads.
audiences.investors: Late-stage leads can bring EU co-investment into large rounds; growth funds above the ETCI size thresholds can seek fund-of-funds commitments from the EIF.
audiences.corporates: EU instruments increasingly sit in the same cap tables as corporate investors in strategic tech; check EU investment safeguards on IP and change of control in deal terms.
audiences.ecosystem: Track whether institutional investors' declared intentions (over €8bn) turn into signed commitments; that is the test of the pact.

alternatives: Large rounds also rose with the AI investment cycle and a few mega-rounds; EU participation in them may reflect selection of already-attractive companies rather than additional capital.
limitations: Round dates in the dataset can differ from instrument announcements (ICEYE appears dated 9 June 2026 in the dataset; the EQT announcement is 5 August 2026).
Fund-of-funds investments are invisible at round level.
Public investors are counted only when the announcement names them.

records.author: TechCap Intelligence analyst desk, drafted with AI assistance (Claude)
records.title: AI Act after the Digital Omnibus: obligations arrive while AI funding surges
records.summary: The AI Act has applied generally since 2 August 2026, while the Digital Omnibus pushed high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028. Over the same 12 months, disclosed venture funding into AI-tagged startups reached €13.3bn, 2.8 times the previous 12 months. The data shows no aggregate deterrent effect, but cannot establish the Act's influence either way.

sections.title: Background
sections.text: The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024 with obligations phased in. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) entered into force on 27 July 2026.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)

facts.text: Prohibited practices and AI-literacy obligations have applied since 2 February 2025 and general-purpose AI model obligations since 2 August 2025; the Act applies generally from 2 August 2026.

sources.title: AI Act – Shaping Europe's digital future
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)

facts.text: After the Digital Omnibus, high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 (Annex III uses) and 2 August 2028 (AI in Annex I products); SME simplifications are extended to small mid-caps.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)

facts.text: From 2 August 2026 the AI Office and national authorities enforce the Act, including transparency obligations and the Commission's powers over the most advanced general-purpose AI models, with fines of up to 3% of global turnover.

sources.title: Commission: AI Act enforcement and transparency obligations start

calculations.text: Disclosed venture funding into AI-tagged European startups was €13.25bn in the 12 months to 9 November 2026, up from €4.69bn in the previous 12 months (+183%), against +26% for the whole market.
calculations.method: Equity rounds tagged AI (a round tagged with two sectors counts in both), rolling 365-day windows. Source: TechCap funding dataset (Tech.eu Funding Explorer, CC BY 4.0, plus multi-source confirmed rounds), disclosed rounds to 9 Nov 2026

calculations.text: In the 12 months after the Act entered into force (Aug 2024 – Jul 2025), funding into AI and Software fell 17% compared with the 12 months before, while the whole market fell 24%: 10% better than the market.
calculations.method: Event window: 12 calendar months before vs after August 2024, AI ∪ Software tagged equity rounds vs all equity rounds.

interpretation: At aggregate level the data is not consistent with the Act having deterred AI investment in Europe; AI funding has outpaced the market both after entry into force and in the past year.
The postponement of high-risk obligations reduces near-term compliance cost for most startups; the main 2026 obligations for typical AI startups are transparency and general-purpose-model rules.
hypotheses: Compliance-related due diligence may shift investment towards AI applications outside Annex III high-risk uses before December 2027. Not yet testable with the current sector tags.

audiences.founders: Transparency duties (disclosure, labelling and machine-readable marking of AI-generated content) apply now; high-risk obligations give a runway to December 2027 or August 2028 depending on the use case.
audiences.investors: Add AI Act classification (prohibited / high-risk / transparency / GPAI dependency) to technical due diligence; the timeline shift lowers near-term compliance risk but not the 2027–2028 cliff.
audiences.corporates: Corporates deploying startup AI in high-risk uses will need conformity evidence from suppliers from December 2027.
audiences.ecosystem: Sandboxes and SME simplifications are where support organisations can lower compliance cost for early-stage companies.

alternatives: The global generative-AI investment cycle, a handful of very large rounds and falling interest rates explain most of the movement in AI funding; any effect of the Act is likely small relative to these.
More rounds are tagged AI over time (3.5% of all rounds in 2024, 10.4% in 2026), partly because more companies describe themselves as AI companies.
limitations: Sector tags come from the funding dataset, not from AI Act risk categories.
Announced rounds only; event windows are a statistical association, not a causal estimate.

records.title: Capital is moving into EU strategic sectors, unevenly: semiconductors, defence and AI up; energy and health lagging
records.summary: Sectors covered by the STEP platform took 49% of disclosed venture funding in 2026 to date, against 20% in 2021. Within them, semiconductors (+371%), defence (from €0.18bn to €1.96bn) and AI (+183%) far outpaced a market up 26% over the last 12 months, while energy (−32%) and healthtech (−6%) lagged despite heavy policy coverage.

facts.text: STEP (Regulation (EU) 2024/795) steers existing EU programmes towards digital and deep tech, clean and resource-efficient technologies and biotechnologies; defence technologies were added as a fourth STEP sector by Regulation (EU) 2025/2653.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/795 establishing STEP
Second Guidance Note on STEP (C/2025/6798)

facts.text: The EIC STEP Scale Up Defence call received nine applications requesting €175m of equity against a €100m 2026 budget.

sources.title: EIC: STEP Scale Up Defence call submissions

facts.text: Preliminary Invest Europe data (reported by a secondary source) show deeptech venture investment of €8.5bn in H1 2026 (+35%) and defence €2.7bn, against €1.3bn in H1 2025.

sources.title: The Next Web: Invest Europe preliminary H1 2026 data (secondary source)

calculations.text: Share of disclosed venture euros going to rounds tagged with at least one STEP sector (AI, Deeptech, Semiconductors, Cleantech, Energy, Healthtech, Defence): 20.1% in 2021, 24.4% in 2022, 50.5% in 2023, 39.8% in 2024, 40.7% in 2025, 49.2% in 2026 to date.
calculations.method: Equity rounds; a round counts once if any of its sector tags is a STEP sector. Source: TechCap funding dataset (Tech.eu Funding Explorer, CC BY 4.0, plus multi-source confirmed rounds), disclosed rounds to 9 Nov 2026

calculations.text: Last 12 months vs previous 12 months: Semiconductors €2.38bn (+371%), Defence €1.96bn (vs €0.18bn), AI €13.25bn (+183%), Deeptech €2.64bn (+54%), Cleantech €2.57bn (+13%), Healthtech €7.78bn (−6%), Energy €3.07bn (−32%); whole market +26%.
calculations.method: Rolling 365-day windows to 9 Nov 2026; a round tagged with two sectors counts in both.

calculations.text: Healthtech is the sector where EU-level investors are named most often (128 rounds since 2021), followed by Deeptech (55) and Energy (51).
calculations.method: Rounds naming an EU institution or instrument, by sector tag, 2021 – 9 Nov 2026.

interpretation: Policy attention and capital are aligned in semiconductors, AI and, most recently, defence. In energy and healthtech, which policy covers heavily and where EU investors are most active, private venture funding is falling relative to the market: these are the clearest gaps between strategic priorities and financing activity.
Defence growth starts from a very small base and is concentrated in a few large rounds.
hypotheses: Energy and climate hardware may be shifting from venture equity to project finance, grants and debt (e.g. Innovation Fund auctions), which this equity measure would not capture.

audiences.founders: In energy and healthtech, EU instruments (EIC, Innovation Fund) are a larger part of the available capital than the venture market alone suggests; plan public and private rounds together.
audiences.investors: Relative weakness in energy and healthtech valuations alongside sustained EU support may offer entry points; momentum sectors (AI, semiconductors, defence) are crowded.
audiences.corporates: Corporate venture in energy and health can fill a private-capital gap that EU programmes are already de-risking.
audiences.ecosystem: Gap sectors are where matchmaking between EU-backed companies and private leads is most needed.

alternatives: Sector tagging drift: AI and Deeptech tags are applied to a larger share of rounds in later years, which lifts strategic-sector shares regardless of investment behaviour.
Interest rates and the global AI and defence cycles drive most of these moves; STEP itself creates no new money.
limitations: Grants and debt are excluded from venture totals.
Shares are sensitive to a few mega-rounds in any year.

records.author: TechCap Intelligence analyst desk, drafted with AI assistance (Claude)
records.title: Public co-investors cluster at Series B, and EU-backed rounds almost always have private partners
records.summary: Since 2021, 17% of disclosed Series B rounds name a public investor (EU-level or national), compared with 8% of pre-seed rounds. Of the 354 venture rounds naming an EU-level investor, 68% also name at least one private investor, and their median size is €12.4M against €4.0M for all disclosed venture rounds.

facts.text: The EIC says the EIC Fund has invested in more than 360 deep-tech companies since June 2020 and that over €3.5 of additional investment has followed per €1 it invested directly.

sources.title: EIC: updated EIC Fund Investment Guidelines

calculations.text: Share of rounds naming an EU-level or national public investor, 2021 – 9 Nov 2026: Pre-Seed 8.2%, Seed 9.9%, Series A 13.0%, Series B 17.1%, Series C 12.8%, Series D+ 14.8%, Growth/Late 9.4%; grants 41.3%; venture debt 15.8%.
calculations.method: Investor names matched against published EU and national public-investor rules; rounds without a stated stage excluded. Source: TechCap funding dataset (Tech.eu Funding Explorer, CC BY 4.0, plus multi-source confirmed rounds), disclosed rounds to 9 Nov 2026

calculations.text: EU-level investors named: EIC/EIC Fund in 303 rounds, EIB in 135, other Commission programmes in 46, EIF in 17.
calculations.method: Same matching; a round can name several bodies.

calculations.text: Of 354 venture rounds naming an EU-level investor, 240 (68%) name at least one private investor; median EU-backed venture round €12.4M vs €4.0M for all disclosed venture rounds.
calculations.method: Placeholder names such as 'existing investors' are not counted as private investors.

interpretation: Public money in the round data is concentrated where European private capital is thinnest relative to need: Series A to Series B, and in grant-plus-equity deep-tech rounds.
Co-investment with named private investors is the norm, which is consistent with the EIC's leverage claim, but the round data cannot measure leverage itself.
hypotheses: EU participation may raise round sizes (signalling), or EU investors may select companies already able to raise large rounds. Comparing companies just above and below EIC selection thresholds would help separate the two; that data is not public.

audiences.founders: Public co-investors are most common at Series B; a strong private lead is still expected alongside them.
audiences.investors: EU and national promotional investors are frequent co-investors at A/B; they can extend round size without taking the lead.
audiences.corporates: Rounds with EU investors are larger on average; corporate investors entering them meet EU investment safeguards.
audiences.ecosystem: Earlier-stage public participation is comparatively thin, at about one round in ten at pre-seed and seed.

alternatives: Larger EU-backed rounds may reflect sector mix (deep tech needs more capital) rather than any effect of EU participation.
limitations: A public-to-private ratio cannot be computed: announcements rarely state each investor's share.
National promotional banks are counted as national even when they deploy EU funds.
Public investors not named in announcements are missed.

records.title: What November 2026's policy calendar means for founders, investors, corporates and ecosystem builders
records.summary: The next six months bring hard EU funding deadlines (STEP Scale Up on 25 Nov 2026, EIC Accelerator from 20 Jan 2027, Eurostars on 4 Mar 2027) and live compliance duties (CRA reporting, AI Act transparency). EU Inc. and the next EU budget remain open, so they should not yet drive company planning.

facts.text: EIC STEP Scale Up next batch cut-off: 25 November 2026; 2027 cut-offs on 28 January, 29 April, 6 September and 24 November.

sources.title: EIC STEP Scale Up

facts.text: EIC Accelerator full-proposal cut-offs in 2027: 20 January, 17 March, 1 September and 4 November; the 2027 EIC Work Programme makes €1.8bn available.

sources.title: EIC Accelerator
EIC launches €1.8 billion in funding for 2027

facts.text: Eurostars Call 12 opens on 17 December 2026 with a submission deadline of 4 March 2027.

sources.title: Eurostars programme page (Bulgarian National Innovation Fund)

facts.text: InvestEU equity: fund managers (not startups) can apply to the EIF call for expression of interest until 30 June 2027.

sources.title: EIF: InvestEU Equity products

facts.text: Since 11 September 2026, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform under the Cyber Resilience Act.

sources.title: Commission: CRA reporting

facts.text: EU Inc. (28th regime): the Council adopted its position on 23 October 2026, but Parliament's JURI committee failed to vote on its draft report on 19 October, so negotiations between the institutions have not started.

sources.title: EPRS briefing on the 28th regime proposal
Euronews: EU Inc. – Council position and JURI vote (secondary source)

facts.text: The Council presidency's MFF 2028–2034 negotiating box (10 October 2026) contains only bracketed, non-agreed figures, including €180.4bn for a European Competitiveness Fund and €140bn for Horizon Europe.

sources.title: Council: MFF 2028-2034 negotiating box (ST 13922/26)

facts.text: A Chips Act 2.0 proposal (3 June 2026) that would repeal and replace the 2023 Chips Act is pending.

sources.title: Proposal for a Chips Act 2.0

interpretation: Near-term opportunities are deadline-driven and concentrated in deep tech; regulatory changes that are still being negotiated (EU Inc., the next budget, Chips Act 2.0) are signals, not plans.

audiences.founders: Deep-tech companies raising €50–150M should target the 25 November STEP Scale Up cut-off or the January 2027 batch; earlier-stage companies should prepare for the 20 January 2027 EIC Accelerator cut-off. Hardware and software sellers in the EU must already meet CRA incident-reporting duties. Do not plan corporate structures around EU Inc. until the Parliament has a position.
audiences.investors: VC and growth managers can apply for InvestEU equity commitments until 30 June 2027 and position for ETCI 2.0. Expect more EU co-investment in large deep-tech rounds through the Scaleup Europe Fund and STEP Scale Up.
audiences.corporates: Chips Act 2.0 and the defence opening of EIC equity widen the set of EU-backed companies in strategic supply chains; review co-investment and procurement opportunities.
audiences.ecosystem: Help companies prepare for the January–March 2027 deadlines; the post-2027 budget (European Competitiveness Fund, Horizon Europe) is still under negotiation and its figures are not agreed.

limitations: Deadlines are copied from official pages on 9 November 2026 and can change; always confirm on the programme page before applying.
The Eurostars dates rest on an official national agency page because the Eureka page could not be retrieved.
